quiz.explain: Hardening reduces the attack surface by disabling unneeded features and enforcing a secure configuration baseline. Applying CVE fixes is patching, and password resets and encryption are separate controls.

videos.title: SQL Injection
videos.summary: Messer explains how unsanitised input can alter the meaning of a database query, why it remains one of the most damaging web flaws, and how parameterised queries stop it.
videos.deepDive:
SQL injection (SQLi) happens when an application builds a database query by pasting user input directly into the query text. Because the database cannot tell the difference between the developer's intended command and text the user supplied, carefully chosen input changes what the query does. The root cause is mixing untrusted data with trusted command structure, the same root cause behind most injection attacks.

A concrete, illustrative example. Suppose a login checks credentials with a query conceptually built as: select the user where username equals the typed username and password equals the typed password. If the application simply glues the typed text into that string, a user who types ' OR '1'='1 into the username field turns the condition into something that is always true, so the database returns a row and the application concludes the login succeeded without a valid password. That single classic string, ' OR '1'='1, is the canonical demonstration of why concatenating input is dangerous: the input broke out of the data and became logic. Depending on how the application is written, injection can also be used to read data the user should never see (dumping a whole customer table), to modify or delete records, or in badly configured systems to reach the operating system.

Why is it still everywhere? Databases sit behind almost every application and hold the most valuable data, so the payoff is huge, and the flawed pattern of string-building queries is easy to write and appears in countless legacy applications and tutorials. It consistently ranks among the top web-application risks.

How a SOC analyst detects it: web-server and application logs show query strings or form parameters containing SQL syntax such as single quotes, UNION SELECT, comment markers or OR 1=1; a web application firewall (WAF) logs and blocks such patterns; a sudden spike in database errors or unusually large result sets can indicate probing or data extraction; and database activity monitoring flags queries that read entire tables from a web account that normally reads one row. Blind SQL injection, where the app returns no visible error, shows up as many near-identical requests that differ only slightly, probing the database one true/false answer at a time.

Mitigation has a clear best answer for the exam: parameterised queries (also called prepared statements), where the query structure is fixed and the input is passed separately as data that can never be interpreted as command. Stored procedures used correctly and object-relational mappers help for the same reason. Supporting controls include strict input validation (allow-list what is acceptable), least-privilege database accounts so a web app cannot drop tables, escaping as a fallback, and a WAF as a compensating detective and preventive layer. Never rely on client-side validation alone, since an attacker bypasses the browser. For GRC, this belongs in secure-SDLC standards, code review and application security testing (SAST and DAST) before release.

keyTerms.def: Inserting crafted input into an application so it alters the SQL query the application sends to its database.
A query whose structure is fixed and whose inputs are passed separately as data, so input can never become command; the primary SQLi fix.
Another name for a parameterised query, precompiled with placeholders for user-supplied values.
Checking that input matches an expected format or allow-list before the application uses it.
SQLi where the application returns no visible error or data, so the attacker infers results from true/false behaviour.
A filter that inspects HTTP traffic and blocks known malicious patterns such as injection payloads.
A database login granted only the minimum rights the application needs, limiting the damage of a successful injection.

examTips: The single best answer to prevent SQL injection is parameterised queries or prepared statements; pick it over input validation or a WAF when both appear.
Input like ' OR '1'='1 or a UNION SELECT in a form field or URL parameter is the giveaway for SQLi.
A WAF and least-privilege database accounts are compensating and defence-in-depth controls, not the root-cause fix.
Client-side validation alone never stops injection because attackers bypass the browser; validation must be server-side.
Blind SQLi shows up in logs as many similar requests probing one true/false answer at a time.
videos.realWorld: For a bank's customer-facing web and mobile back ends, SQL injection is a top risk because success can mean dumping customer records or manipulating balances. A SOC analyst reviewing WAF and application logs looks for injection syntax in parameters and correlates it with database errors or oversized responses. Findings feed the application security team, who fix the code with parameterised queries and add the case to regression tests. GRC requires SAST and DAST in the CI pipeline and secure-coding standards, and where a successful injection exposes personal data, drives NDPA breach handling and CBN reporting.

quiz.q: A penetration tester enters ' OR '1'='1 into a login form's username field and is logged in without a valid password. Which vulnerability does this demonstrate, and what is the primary fix?
quiz.explain: Input that changes the query's logic so authentication always passes is SQL injection, and the root-cause fix is parameterised queries that separate data from command. Output encoding addresses XSS, bounds checking addresses overflows, and locking addresses races.

quiz.q: An application already uses a web application firewall that blocks many injection patterns, but the security team wants to eliminate SQL injection at its root. What should they do?
options: Rewrite queries to use parameterised statements
quiz.explain: A WAF is a compensating filter that can be bypassed; parameterised queries remove the underlying flaw by ensuring input is treated as data. More WAFs, password length and at-rest encryption do not fix the injection itself.

quiz.q: Why is relying only on JavaScript validation in the browser insufficient to prevent SQL injection?
options: An attacker can bypass the browser and send requests directly to the server
quiz.explain: Client-side checks are easily bypassed by sending crafted requests straight to the server with a tool, so validation and parameterisation must happen server-side. The other statements misrepresent how JavaScript and databases work.

videos.title: Cross-site Scripting
videos.summary: Messer explains how a web application that reflects or stores untrusted input can end up running an attacker's script in other users' browsers, and how output encoding and CSP stop it.
videos.deepDive:
Cross-site scripting (XSS) is an injection flaw in web applications where an attacker gets their script to run in the browser of another user of the site. The victim's browser trusts anything that appears to come from the site it is visiting, so an attacker's script inherits that trust: it can read the session cookie, act as the user, capture keystrokes on the page, or rewrite what the page shows. The root cause is the familiar one: the application takes untrusted input and includes it in a web page without neutralising it, so the browser treats attacker text as executable code rather than as content.

There are three types the exam expects. Stored (persistent) XSS is the most dangerous: the malicious script is saved on the server, for example in a forum comment, a support-ticket field or a profile name, and then served to every user who views that content. One planted comment can hit thousands of victims. Reflected XSS bounces the script off the server in a single response: the payload is placed in a crafted link or form, and when the victim clicks the link the server echoes the input straight back into the page and it runs. This one usually requires tricking the victim into clicking, so it is often combined with phishing. DOM-based XSS happens entirely in the browser when client-side JavaScript takes attacker-controlled input from the URL or page and writes it into the page unsafely, without the server ever processing it.

A worked example of the classic impact: a banking web app displays a support message field without sanitising it. An attacker submits a message containing a small script that reads the logged-in user's session cookie and sends it to the attacker's server. Every support agent who opens that ticket unknowingly runs the script, and their session identifiers are harvested, letting the attacker ride their authenticated sessions. XSS is frequently a stepping stone to session hijacking and account takeover.

How a SOC analyst detects it: application and WAF logs show input parameters containing script tags, event-handler attributes or JavaScript URIs; unexpected outbound requests from users' browsers to an unfamiliar domain (the exfiltration endpoint) appear in proxy logs; and a stored-XSS report often starts with users complaining of odd pop-ups or redirects on a legitimate page. Because the script runs in the client, server-side monitoring alone can miss DOM-based cases.

Mitigation, and the exam's preferred answers: context-aware output encoding so that any user data placed into a page is rendered as inert text rather than executed; strong input validation as a supporting layer; a Content Security Policy (CSP) that tells the browser to run scripts only from approved sources, sharply limiting what injected script can do; marking session cookies HttpOnly so script cannot read them and Secure so they travel only over HTTPS; and using framework features and trusted templating that encode by default. A WAF adds a detective and preventive layer. Contrast with SQL injection: SQLi targets the database and is fixed with parameterised queries, while XSS targets other users' browsers and is fixed with output encoding and CSP.

keyTerms.def: A web flaw where an attacker's script runs in another user's browser because the application failed to neutralise untrusted input in a page.
Persistent XSS where the malicious script is saved on the server and served to every user who views the affected content.
XSS where the payload is echoed back in a single response, usually via a crafted link the victim must click.
XSS that occurs in client-side JavaScript writing untrusted input into the page, without the server processing it.
Converting user data into inert display characters so the browser renders it as text, not executable code; the primary XSS fix.
A browser policy restricting which sources of scripts and content are allowed to run, limiting the impact of injected script.
A cookie flag that prevents client-side scripts from reading the cookie, protecting session identifiers from XSS theft.
Taking over a user's authenticated session, a common goal of stealing session cookies via XSS.

examTips: The primary XSS fix is context-aware output encoding; Content Security Policy and HttpOnly cookies are strong supporting controls.
Stored XSS affects everyone who views the content and is worst; reflected XSS needs a victim to click a crafted link; DOM-based happens in the browser.
Distinguish from SQL injection by the target: XSS runs script in a user's browser, SQLi manipulates the database.
A common XSS goal is stealing session cookies for session hijacking; HttpOnly cookies block that specific theft.
Reflected XSS is often paired with phishing to get the victim to click the malicious link.
videos.realWorld: For a bank's online and mobile web front ends, XSS can lead to session hijacking of both customers and staff, so it is a priority in application security testing. A SOC analyst may catch it as proxy logs showing users' browsers posting session data to an unknown domain, or as a stored-XSS report after users see strange behaviour on a legitimate page. The response is to remove the stored payload, force affected sessions to re-authenticate, and have the app team add output encoding and a Content Security Policy. GRC requires these defences in secure-coding standards and verifies them through DAST in the release pipeline.

quiz.q: An attacker submits a support-ticket comment containing a script. Every agent who later opens that ticket has the script run in their browser, sending their session cookies to an external server. Which type of XSS is this?
quiz.explain: The script is saved on the server and served to every user who views the content, which is stored (persistent) XSS, the most damaging form. Reflected and DOM-based XSS do not persist server-side, and SQL injection targets the database, not the browser.

quiz.q: Which control is the PRIMARY fix for cross-site scripting?
options: Context-aware output encoding of user data in pages
quiz.explain: Encoding user-supplied data so the browser renders it as inert text is the root-cause XSS fix. Parameterised queries fix SQL injection, disk encryption protects data at rest, and disabling HTTPS would weaken security.

quiz.q: Setting session cookies as HttpOnly specifically protects against which XSS impact?
options: Client-side script reading the session cookie to hijack the session
quiz.explain: HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie, so an XSS payload cannot steal the session identifier for session hijacking. It does not affect overflows, database injection or password guessing.

videos.title: Hardware Vulnerabilities
videos.summary: Messer explains vulnerabilities in the physical and firmware layer, including firmware flaws, end-of-life and legacy hardware, and the difficulty of patching devices you cannot easily update.
videos.deepDive:
Below the operating system sits firmware and physical hardware, and flaws there are among the hardest to find and fix. A hardware vulnerability is a weakness in a device's firmware, chip design or physical construction. It matters because these components run before and beneath the OS, so a compromise there can survive reinstalling the operating system and can be invisible to software running on top. The exam focuses on the practical categories: firmware flaws, end-of-life and legacy hardware, and the general difficulty of updating embedded devices.

Firmware is the low-level code baked into devices: the system UEFI or BIOS, network cards, drives, routers, IP cameras, point-of-sale terminals and countless Internet-of-Things devices. Firmware is written by many vendors, updated rarely, and often shipped with weak defaults or hard-coded credentials. A vulnerability in firmware can give an attacker persistent, deep control. Some firmware attacks target the boot process itself, which is why secure boot and measured boot with a Trusted Platform Module exist to verify that only trusted firmware and boot code run.

End-of-life hardware is equipment the manufacturer no longer supports, so no firmware fixes are issued for new flaws. This is the physical counterpart of the unsupported-software problem, and it is very real in banking: ATMs, card-reader terminals and network appliances stay in service long after support ends because replacing them is expensive and disruptive. Legacy hardware may still be supported but is old enough to lack modern security features. Either way, the device becomes a permanent soft spot.

A worked example: a bank runs a fleet of point-of-sale and ATM devices whose firmware has a known flaw and whose vendor stopped issuing updates two years ago. An attacker with the right access can implant persistent code in the firmware that survives a full software reimage, letting them skim card data indefinitely. Because it lives below the OS, ordinary antivirus and even EDR may never see it.

How a SOC analyst or security engineer deals with it: maintain a hardware and firmware inventory, subscribe to vendor and CERT advisories for firmware CVEs, and monitor for the anomalies you can see, such as an embedded device making unexpected network connections or a system failing boot-integrity attestation. Because you often cannot patch these devices quickly, detection leans on network monitoring and segmentation.

Mitigation combines lifecycle and compensating controls. Keep firmware updated where the vendor supports it, and verify signed firmware images. Use secure boot and TPM-based integrity checks to detect boot-level tampering. Retire or replace end-of-life hardware on a planned lifecycle. Where a device cannot be replaced yet, isolate it on its own network segment, restrict what it can talk to, and monitor it closely as a compensating control. Physical security matters too, since many firmware compromises need physical or supply-chain access. For GRC, the deliverables are an asset lifecycle policy, a hardware and firmware inventory, and documented exceptions with compensating controls for anything past end-of-life.

keyTerms.def: A weakness in a device's firmware, chip design or physical construction that an attacker can exploit.
Low-level code embedded in a device that controls its basic functions and runs beneath the operating system.
Equipment the manufacturer no longer supports, so no firmware or security fixes will be issued.
Older equipment that may still function but lacks modern security features and controls.
A mechanism that verifies firmware and boot code signatures so only trusted software loads at startup.
A hardware chip that stores keys and supports integrity measurement and attestation of the boot process.
A vendor-supplied, ideally signed, update to a device's embedded code that fixes flaws or adds features.

examTips: Firmware flaws run beneath the OS, so they can persist through a reinstall and evade antivirus; the answer often involves secure boot, TPM attestation or firmware updates.
End-of-life hardware is the physical version of unsupported software: no fixes will come, so isolate or replace it.
When a vulnerable device cannot be patched or replaced, the exam wants network segmentation and monitoring as compensating controls.
Secure boot and a TPM detect boot-level and firmware tampering; associate them with hardware integrity.
Many firmware compromises need physical or supply-chain access, so physical security is relevant here.
videos.realWorld: Banks operate large fleets of long-lived hardware such as ATMs, POS terminals and network gear, so firmware and end-of-life risk is a standing agenda item. Security engineers track firmware advisories, verify signed images before flashing, and use secure boot and TPM attestation on servers. Devices past end-of-life that cannot be replaced immediately are placed on isolated segments with tight allow-lists and heavy monitoring, and the SOC watches for those devices making connections they should not. GRC maintains the asset lifecycle policy and the exception register that CBN examiners routinely ask to see.

quiz.q: An attacker implants malicious code in the firmware of a bank's ATM. After the ATM's operating system is fully reinstalled, the malicious behaviour returns. Why?
options: The ATM has a weak password
The reinstall failed to copy files
Firmware runs beneath the OS, so it persists through an OS reimage
quiz.explain: Firmware sits below the operating system and is not touched by reinstalling the OS, so firmware-resident code survives a reimage and can evade software security tools. The other options do not explain persistence beneath the OS.

quiz.q: A vulnerable network appliance is past its end-of-life and cannot be replaced for six months. What is the BEST interim mitigation?
options: Isolate it on its own segment with strict allow-lists and enhanced monitoring
Give it a longer administrator password
Ignore it since it still works
quiz.explain: When an unpatchable device must remain, network segmentation, restricted communication and close monitoring act as compensating controls until replacement. Ignoring it accepts unmanaged risk, and reimaging or a longer password does not address unpatched firmware flaws.

quiz.q: Which technologies are specifically designed to detect tampering with firmware or the boot process?
options: Secure boot and a Trusted Platform Module
A web application firewall and CSP
quiz.explain: Secure boot verifies boot-code signatures and a TPM supports integrity measurement and attestation, together detecting firmware and boot tampering. The other pairs address web injection and concurrency, not firmware integrity.

videos.title: Virtualization Vulnerabilities
videos.summary: Messer explains the risks unique to virtualised environments, including VM escape, resource contention between guests, and VM sprawl that leaves unmanaged machines.
videos.deepDive:
Virtualization lets one physical server run many isolated virtual machines (VMs), each with its own OS, coordinated by a hypervisor. The whole model depends on that isolation holding, so virtualization vulnerabilities are the flaws that threaten it. Because a single physical host may run dozens of a bank's servers, a flaw at the virtualization layer can have outsized impact.

The most serious risk is VM escape: an attacker who has compromised one guest VM exploits a flaw in the hypervisor to break out of that VM and reach the host or other VMs on the same host. In a shared or multi-tenant environment this is the nightmare scenario, because it collapses the isolation that separates one customer or one workload from another. VM escape flaws are rare and highly valued, but they do occur, which is why hypervisor patching is treated as critical.

Other named risks: resource contention and denial of service between guests, where one VM consumes so much CPU, memory or disk I/O that neighbouring VMs on the host are starved, sometimes called a noisy-neighbour problem and exploitable to degrade a co-tenant. VM sprawl is an operational vulnerability: because spinning up a VM is so easy, organisations accumulate forgotten machines that are unpatched, unmonitored and still connected, each an easy foothold. Insecure snapshots and templates spread problems fast: a golden image with an embedded flaw or credential is copied into every new VM, and a rolled-back snapshot can silently reintroduce a vulnerability that was already patched or reactivate old accounts. There is also the risk of weak isolation and shared components such as virtual networks and management interfaces that, if misconfigured, let VMs see traffic or resources they should not.

A worked example: a fintech runs customer workloads and an internal admin VM on the same physical host. An attacker compromises the low-value customer-facing VM, then exploits a hypervisor flaw to escape onto the host, from where they reach the admin VM. The lesson the exam draws is that sensitive and untrusted workloads should not share a host without strong controls, and that the hypervisor must be patched like the crown jewel it is.

How a SOC analyst engages: monitor the hypervisor and virtualization management console logs, alert on unexpected VM creation or configuration changes, track VM inventory to spot sprawl, and watch for a guest attempting hypervisor-level operations. Cloud and virtualization posture-management tools flag insecure configurations and orphaned machines.

Mitigation: patch the hypervisor promptly and keep guest tools updated; keep the hypervisor attack surface minimal by treating the management interface as highly sensitive and restricting access to it; separate workloads by sensitivity, ideally not co-locating untrusted and sensitive VMs on the same host; control VM sprawl with lifecycle management, tagging and decommissioning; secure and patch golden images and control snapshot use; and segment virtual networks. For GRC, this is part of cloud and infrastructure security standards, configuration baselines and asset management.

keyTerms.def: Software that creates and manages virtual machines and enforces isolation between them on a physical host.
A software-based computer with its own OS running on shared physical hardware under a hypervisor.
Breaking out of a guest VM by exploiting the hypervisor to reach the host or other VMs, defeating isolation.
The uncontrolled accumulation of virtual machines, many forgotten, unpatched and unmonitored.
One VM consuming shared host resources to the point that co-located VMs are degraded or denied service.
A saved state of a VM; rolling back can reintroduce old vulnerabilities or accounts if misused.
A master VM template copied to create new machines; a flaw in it propagates to every copy.

examTips: VM escape is the headline virtualization risk: a guest breaking out to the host or other guests; the control is hypervisor patching and workload separation.
VM sprawl is an operational vulnerability of forgotten, unpatched machines; the answer is lifecycle management and inventory.
Rolling back a snapshot can reintroduce a patched vulnerability or a disabled account; manage snapshots carefully.
Do not co-locate untrusted and highly sensitive workloads on the same host without strong isolation.
The virtualization management interface is highly sensitive; restricting access to it is a key control.
videos.realWorld: Banks and fintechs run heavily virtualised data centres and cloud tenancies, so the SOC monitors hypervisor and virtualization-console logs for unexpected VM creation, configuration drift and signs of a guest probing the host. Posture-management tooling flags orphaned VMs from sprawl and insecure templates. When a hypervisor vulnerability with escape potential is announced, it is patched as an emergency because a single host may run many production systems. GRC sets the configuration baselines, the workload-separation policy for sensitive systems, and the VM lifecycle standard, and evidences them for auditors.

quiz.q: An attacker compromises a low-value customer VM and then exploits a flaw in the hypervisor to gain access to the physical host and other VMs running on it. What is this attack called?
quiz.explain: Breaking out of a guest VM through a hypervisor flaw to reach the host or neighbouring VMs is a VM escape, which defeats virtualization isolation. Sprawl, snapshot rollback and resource contention are other virtualization risks that do not describe breaking isolation this way.

quiz.q: A cloud audit finds dozens of running virtual machines that no team recognises, none patched in over a year. Which virtualization risk is this, and what is the fix?
options: VM sprawl; VM lifecycle management and inventory
quiz.explain: Forgotten, unmanaged VMs are VM sprawl, addressed by lifecycle management, tagging, inventory and decommissioning. It is not an escape or contention issue, and disabling snapshots does not address orphaned machines.

quiz.q: Why can rolling back a VM to an older snapshot create a security problem?
options: It can reintroduce a vulnerability or re-enable an account that had been remediated
It encrypts all data by default
quiz.explain: A snapshot captures an earlier state, so reverting can undo patches and re-enable removed or disabled accounts, silently restoring old risk. The other statements are not accurate descriptions of snapshot rollback.

videos.title: Cloud-specific Vulnerabilities
videos.summary: Messer explains the vulnerabilities that arise specifically from cloud computing, including misconfiguration, the shared responsibility model, insecure APIs, and identity and access weaknesses.
videos.deepDive:
Moving to the cloud does not remove security work; it changes where the risk lives. Cloud-specific vulnerabilities are the weaknesses that come from how cloud platforms are built and operated. The single most common and damaging one is misconfiguration, especially of storage and access. The exam's canonical example is a cloud storage bucket accidentally set to public, exposing customer data to anyone on the internet; countless real breaches have come from exactly this. Cloud makes powerful configuration changes a click or an API call away, so a small mistake can expose enormous amounts of data instantly.

Underlying much of this is the shared responsibility model. The cloud provider secures the underlying infrastructure (the data centres, the hardware, the hypervisor), while the customer remains responsible for securing what they put on top: data, configuration, identities, access policies and application code. Breaches often trace to a customer assuming the provider covered something the customer actually owned. Knowing which side owns what for IaaS, PaaS and SaaS is exam material and real-world essential.

Other cloud-specific risks: insecure APIs, because everything in the cloud is driven by APIs, and an unauthenticated, over-permissioned or poorly validated API is a direct path in; weak identity and access management, where over-privileged accounts, unused access keys, missing MFA and long-lived credentials let a single compromised identity reach far; improper key and secret management, such as access keys committed to a public code repository, which attackers actively scan for; insufficient logging and monitoring, where cloud audit logs are not enabled or not watched; and account or tenant isolation concerns in multi-tenant services. Because cloud environments change constantly and can be built by many teams, configuration drift is a persistent problem.

A worked example rooted in Nigerian fintech reality: a fast-growing fintech's developer creates a storage bucket for KYC documents and, to move quickly, leaves it publicly readable, then commits the cloud access key to a public GitHub repository. Automated scanners find the key within minutes, and the open bucket exposes customers' ID cards and BVNs. Two classic cloud vulnerabilities, storage misconfiguration and leaked secrets, combine into a serious personal-data breach with NDPA implications.

How a SOC analyst engages: cloud-native logging (such as audit trails of API calls) and a cloud security posture management (CSPM) tool are the main instruments. They flag public buckets, over-permissive identity policies, disabled logging, and anomalous API activity such as mass downloads or access from an unusual location. Alerts on new access-key creation, root or admin usage, and impossible-travel logins are standard.

Mitigation: apply secure configuration baselines and use CSPM to detect drift automatically; enforce least privilege on identities and use short-lived credentials and MFA everywhere; keep secrets in a managed secrets vault, never in code, and scan repositories for leaked keys; enable and centralise cloud audit logging; and understand and document the shared-responsibility split for every service used. For GRC, this is cloud governance: configuration standards, identity governance, and third-party assurance from the provider.

keyTerms.def: An insecure cloud setting, most often overly permissive storage or access, that exposes data or resources.
The division of security duties in which the provider secures the infrastructure and the customer secures data, configuration, identities and access.
A cloud application programming interface that is unauthenticated, over-permissioned or poorly validated, offering a direct attack path.
Tooling that continuously checks cloud configurations against best practice and flags risky settings and drift.
Securely storing and rotating credentials and keys in a vault rather than embedding them in code or configuration.
Granting cloud identities only the permissions they need, using short-lived credentials and MFA to limit blast radius.
The gradual divergence of a cloud environment from its secure baseline as many changes accumulate over time.

examTips: Misconfiguration, especially a public storage bucket, is the most common cloud vulnerability; CSPM and secure baselines are the answers.
The shared responsibility model puts data, configuration, identity and access on the customer; the provider secures the underlying infrastructure.
Leaked access keys in public code repositories are a classic cloud breach path; store secrets in a vault and scan repos.
Cloud IAM answers favour least privilege, MFA and short-lived credentials over long-lived access keys.
If cloud audit logging is disabled, you cannot detect or investigate; enabling and centralising it is a key control.
videos.realWorld: Nigerian fintechs are cloud-first, so cloud misconfiguration and leaked secrets are among their most likely breach causes. A SOC analyst watches cloud audit logs and CSPM alerts for public buckets, new admin keys, disabled logging and impossible-travel logins, and jumps on any secret detected in a code repository. When KYC or BVN data is exposed, the incident becomes an NDPA-reportable personal-data breach and, for a licensed institution, a CBN reporting matter. GRC owns cloud governance: baselines, identity governance, secrets policy, and mapping the shared-responsibility split for every service in use.

quiz.q: A fintech developer stores customer KYC documents in a cloud storage bucket left publicly readable and commits the cloud access key to a public code repository. Which TWO cloud-specific vulnerabilities are present?
quiz.explain: A public bucket is a storage misconfiguration and a committed access key is a leaked secret, both classic cloud vulnerabilities that together expose customer data. The other pairs describe virtualization, web and memory or concurrency flaws not present here.

quiz.q: Under the shared responsibility model for infrastructure-as-a-service, which of the following is the CUSTOMER's responsibility?
options: Configuring access controls and securing their data
quiz.explain: Customers are responsible for their data, configurations, identities and access, while the provider secures the physical facilities, hardware and hypervisor. Confusing this split is a common cause of cloud breaches.

quiz.q: Which tool is BEST suited to continuously detect risky cloud settings such as public buckets and over-permissive identities?
options: A cloud security posture management (CSPM) tool
quiz.explain: CSPM continuously evaluates cloud configurations against best practice and flags drift and risky settings. Antivirus scans files, a stack canary is a memory-overflow defence, and a mantrap is a physical control.

videos.title: Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
videos.summary: Messer explains how trust in vendors, service providers and third-party software components creates risk, covering hardware, software and managed-service supply chains.
videos.deepDive:
No organisation builds everything itself. You buy hardware, run third-party software, embed open-source libraries, and hand operations to service providers. A supply chain vulnerability is a weakness that reaches you through one of these trusted relationships. It is dangerous because the compromise arrives pre-trusted: you deliberately gave the vendor access or ran their code, so it sails past defences aimed at outside attackers. The exam splits the supply chain into three parts and expects you to reason about each.

The hardware supply chain covers the risk that devices or components are tampered with before they reach you, counterfeit parts are substituted, or malicious functionality is added during manufacturing or transit. This is hard to detect and is why sensitive buyers use trusted suppliers and validate hardware integrity. The software supply chain is the broadest in practice. Modern applications are assembled from many third-party and open-source components, so a vulnerability or backdoor in one dependency propagates to everyone who uses it. This includes compromised software updates (the SolarWinds pattern), poisoned packages uploaded to public repositories, and typo-squatted package names that trick developers into installing malicious libraries. The 2021 Log4j vulnerability showed how a single widely embedded open-source component can expose a huge fraction of the internet at once. The managed service provider (MSP) supply chain is the third: an MSP or vendor with remote access into many client networks is a high-value target, because compromising the provider gives an attacker a trusted path into all of its customers.

A worked example: a bank uses a third-party provider to manage part of its infrastructure, granting the provider standing remote access. Attackers compromise the provider and use that trusted access to move into the bank's network. Nothing about the bank's own perimeter was breached; the trusted relationship was the vector. This exact pattern has driven major real-world incidents.

How a SOC analyst engages: monitor vendor and MSP remote-access accounts closely, alerting on off-hours use or access from unusual locations; maintain a software bill of materials (SBOM) so that when a component vulnerability like Log4j is announced you can immediately find where it is used; and watch for anomalous behaviour from trusted third-party software or updates. Detection is hard precisely because the activity comes from a trusted source, so behavioural monitoring and least privilege for third parties are central.

Mitigation is largely governance plus technical controls. Perform vendor security assessments and due diligence before onboarding and periodically after. Put security requirements in contracts, including breach notification. Grant third parties least privilege and just-in-time rather than standing access, and monitor everything they do. Require and maintain SBOMs, and verify signatures and hashes on software and updates. Use dependency scanning to catch vulnerable and malicious packages in your own builds. Segment vendor access so a compromised provider cannot reach the whole network. For GRC, this is the heart of third-party risk management, an area regulators including the CBN scrutinise closely for banks.

keyTerms.def: A weakness that reaches an organisation through a trusted vendor, component, service provider or update.
The chain of third-party and open-source components and updates that make up software, any of which can introduce risk.
The danger that compromising a provider with remote access to many clients gives attackers a trusted path into all of them.
An inventory of the components in software that lets an organisation find where a vulnerable component is used.
Evaluating a third party's security posture before and during a relationship to manage the risk they introduce.
Automatically checking third-party libraries used in a build for known vulnerabilities or malicious packages.
Granting vendors only the minimal, ideally just-in-time, access needed rather than broad standing access.

examTips: A trusted vendor, component or update being the way in is a supply-chain attack; recall SolarWinds (updates) and Log4j (open-source component).
An SBOM is what lets you rapidly find every place a newly announced vulnerable component is used.
MSP compromise gives attackers a trusted path into all clients; monitor and least-privilege third-party remote access.
Detection is hard because activity comes from a trusted source, so favour behavioural monitoring, least privilege and segmentation.
For GRC, third-party risk management, vendor assessments and contractual security requirements are the expected answers, and regulators scrutinise them.
videos.realWorld: Banks depend on many vendors and MSPs, and the CBN expects rigorous third-party risk management, so supply-chain risk is a major GRC workstream. A SOC analyst monitors vendor remote-access accounts for off-hours or foreign logins and, when a component flaw such as Log4j breaks, uses the SBOM to locate every affected system for emergency patching. Analysts also watch trusted third-party software for anomalous behaviour after updates. GRC runs vendor security assessments, bakes security and breach-notification clauses into contracts, enforces least-privilege just-in-time vendor access, and evidences all of it for examiners.

quiz.q: Attackers compromise a managed service provider that has standing remote access into many banks and use that access to enter one bank's network, without ever touching the bank's own perimeter defences. Which vulnerability class is this?
quiz.explain: The attack reaches the bank through a trusted service provider relationship, which is a supply-chain vulnerability. The bank's perimeter was not breached directly, and the other options describe web, memory and concurrency flaws.

quiz.q: When a critical vulnerability is announced in a widely used open-source library, which artefact MOST helps an organisation quickly find every affected system?
quiz.explain: An SBOM inventories software components, so it lets teams immediately locate everywhere the vulnerable library is used, as many organisations wished they had during Log4j. A diagram, password policy or firewall rules do not map component usage.

quiz.q: Which control BEST reduces the risk that a compromised vendor account leads to a full network breach?
options: Give the vendor broad standing administrator access for convenience
Grant least-privilege, just-in-time access and monitor and segment vendor activity
Share a single vendor login among all providers
quiz.explain: Least-privilege, just-in-time access with monitoring and segmentation limits what a compromised vendor account can reach and makes misuse visible. Broad standing access, shared logins and disabled logging all increase risk.

videos.title: Misconfiguration Vulnerabilities
videos.summary: Messer explains how insecure settings, default credentials, unnecessary open services and weak permissions create vulnerabilities even when software has no coding flaw.
videos.deepDive:
A misconfiguration vulnerability exists when software or a system is fully patched and free of coding flaws but is set up insecurely. The weakness is in the settings, not the code. Misconfiguration is one of the most common causes of real breaches precisely because it is so easy to introduce: a rushed deployment, a copied setting, a default left in place, or a change made to fix an urgent problem that quietly opens a door. Nothing needs to be hacked; the system was simply left open.

The exam and the field group misconfigurations into recognisable types. Default credentials are the classic case: a device, database or admin console shipped with a known factory username and password that was never changed. Attackers scan the internet for these using published default-password lists, so an unchanged default is often exploited within hours of exposure. Unnecessary open ports and services widen the attack surface: a management port, database port or file-sharing service exposed to the internet when it should be internal-only. Overly permissive access and permissions include world-readable files, a cloud storage bucket set to public, database accounts with far more rights than the application needs, and firewall rules that allow far more than required. Missing or weak security settings cover encryption not enabled, verbose error messages leaking internal details, security headers absent from web servers, and logging turned off. Default or sample content left on servers, such as a default admin page or sample application, can also provide an entry point.

A worked example: during a rushed launch, a fintech deploys a database to the cloud and, to get connectivity working, opens the database port to the internet and keeps the vendor's default administrator password. An attacker running internet-wide scans finds the open port, tries the well-known default credentials, logs in, and copies the customer table. Every element was a configuration choice; the software itself had no vulnerability. This combination, an exposed service plus default credentials, is behind a large share of real data breaches.

How a SOC analyst and security team detect it: vulnerability scanners and configuration-assessment tools flag default credentials, open ports, missing patches-of-configuration and weak settings against a baseline; external attack-surface scans show what is exposed to the internet; cloud posture tools flag public buckets and permissive policies; and log review reveals successful logins with default accounts or access to services that should not be reachable. Benchmarks such as the CIS controls define what secure should look like so drift is measurable.

Mitigation is disciplined configuration management. Change all default credentials before deployment and prefer disabling default accounts. Close or firewall unnecessary ports and disable unused services, following the principle of reducing the attack surface. Apply least privilege to files, accounts and network rules. Enforce secure baselines such as CIS benchmarks and use automation and infrastructure-as-code so systems are built to a known-good standard rather than by hand. Continuously assess for drift with scanning and posture tools. Suppress verbose error messages in production and ensure encryption and logging are on. For GRC, this is configuration-management policy, hardening standards, and regular vulnerability and configuration assessment reported to management.

keyTerms.def: A weakness caused by insecure settings rather than a flaw in the software code itself.
Factory-set usernames and passwords shipped with a product that are exploited when left unchanged.
Closing unnecessary ports and disabling unused services and features to give attackers fewer targets.
Granting more access than needed, such as public storage, world-readable files or over-privileged accounts.
A defined secure configuration standard, such as a CIS benchmark, applied consistently and checked for drift.
The disciplined process of defining, applying and maintaining secure system settings, ideally through automation.
Defining systems and configuration in version-controlled code so they are built consistently to a secure standard.

examTips: Misconfiguration means the software is fine but the settings are insecure; default credentials and open services are the classic examples.
Default credentials are fixed by changing or disabling them before deployment, not by MFA or patching.
Unnecessary open ports and services call for attack-surface reduction: close, firewall or disable them.
Secure baselines like CIS benchmarks and configuration management or infrastructure-as-code are the systematic fixes and the exam's preferred answers.
A public cloud bucket or an over-privileged account is a permissions misconfiguration; least privilege is the control.
videos.realWorld: Misconfiguration is one of the most frequent real-world breach causes at banks and fintechs, usually born of rushed deployments. A SOC and vulnerability-management team run internal and external scans and cloud posture tools to catch default credentials, exposed ports, public buckets and permissive policies, then drive remediation against a baseline. Analysts also review logs for logins using default accounts or access to services that should be internal. GRC sets hardening standards on CIS benchmarks, mandates configuration management and infrastructure-as-code, and reports configuration findings and remediation to leadership and to CBN examiners.

quiz.q: During a rushed launch, a fintech exposes a database port to the internet and leaves the vendor's default administrator password in place. An attacker scans, logs in with the default credentials, and copies customer data. What class of vulnerability is this?
options: A misconfiguration (exposed service plus default credentials)
quiz.explain: The software had no coding flaw; an insecurely exposed service combined with unchanged default credentials is a misconfiguration. It is not a zero-day, and it does not involve memory or browser injection.

quiz.q: Which practice BEST prevents default-credential vulnerabilities across a fleet of newly deployed devices?
options: Change or disable default accounts and passwords before deployment
Open all management ports for convenience
Turn off logging to save space
quiz.explain: Changing or disabling factory default accounts before a device goes live removes the credential an attacker would try first. Verbose errors, open ports and disabled logging all worsen security.

quiz.q: A security team wants to ensure servers are built consistently to a secure standard and to detect when their settings drift. Which combination BEST achieves this?
options: Manual setup by different admins each time
Secure baselines (such as CIS benchmarks) enforced with infrastructure-as-code and continuous configuration assessment
A single annual review with no tooling
quiz.explain: Defining a secure baseline, building systems from version-controlled infrastructure-as-code, and continuously assessing for drift produce consistent, measurable configuration security. Manual, ad hoc setup and password length alone do not address configuration drift.

videos.title: Mobile Device Vulnerabilities
videos.summary: Messer explains vulnerabilities specific to smartphones and tablets, including sideloading, jailbreaking and rooting, insecure connections, and the challenges of securing personal devices at work.
videos.deepDive:
Mobile devices are full computers that hold banking apps, email, authentication tokens and personal data, and they travel with the user onto untrusted networks. Mobile device vulnerabilities are the weaknesses specific to this platform and how people use it. They matter enormously in a country like Nigeria where mobile banking and USSD are primary channels and where a huge share of both legitimate and fraudulent financial activity happens on phones.

Key categories the exam expects. Sideloading is installing apps from outside the official app store. Official stores vet apps imperfectly but do vet them; sideloaded apps bypass that entirely, and a fake banking app or a repackaged legitimate app with added malware is a common way to steal credentials. Jailbreaking (iOS) and rooting (Android) remove the manufacturer's built-in restrictions to gain full control of the device. Users do it for customisation, but it disables core security protections, breaks the app sandbox, and lets malware gain deep access; a rooted device running a banking app is far more exposed. Insecure connections include joining open or rogue Wi-Fi hotspots where traffic can be intercepted, and Bluetooth attacks; a phone that auto-connects to a malicious hotspot in a public place is a real risk. Outdated and unpatched devices are widespread because many cheaper Android phones stop receiving updates quickly, leaving known OS flaws open, which links back to unsupported systems. Weak device security such as no screen lock or a weak PIN means physical loss equals data loss.

Then there is the workplace dimension. Bring your own device (BYOD) mixes personal and corporate data on a device the organisation does not fully control, raising the risk of data leakage and making it hard to enforce policy. The exam contrasts BYOD with COPE (corporate-owned, personally enabled) and CYOD (choose your own device) as deployment models with different control trade-offs. Related risks include excessive app permissions (an app demanding access to contacts, SMS and location it does not need) and SMS-based one-time codes being intercepted, which connects to SIM-swap fraud that is prevalent in the region.

How a SOC analyst engages: a mobile device management (MDM) or unified endpoint management (UEM) platform reports device compliance, flags rooted or jailbroken devices, and enforces policy; alerts fire on a jailbroken device attempting to access corporate resources or a banking app detecting a rooted environment; and fraud systems watch for logins from a device that suddenly shows tampering indicators.

Mitigation: deploy MDM or UEM to enforce encryption, screen locks, patch levels and app policy, and to remotely wipe lost devices; block rooted and jailbroken devices from sensitive apps and resources through attestation; restrict installation to official stores and use app-reputation checks; require a VPN on untrusted networks and discourage auto-connect to open Wi-Fi; keep devices patched and retire those that no longer receive updates; use containerisation to separate corporate and personal data on BYOD; and prefer app-based or hardware authenticators over SMS codes where possible. For GRC, this is mobile-device policy, the BYOD or COPE decision, and acceptable-use standards.

keyTerms.def: Installing apps from outside the official app store, bypassing its vetting and increasing malware risk.
Removing manufacturer restrictions on iOS or Android to gain full control, which disables built-in security protections.
A platform that enforces security policy, compliance and remote wipe on mobile devices, often part of unified endpoint management.
A model where employees use personal devices for work, mixing corporate and personal data on an under-controlled device.
Separating corporate data and apps from personal ones on a device so each can be managed independently.
An app requesting more access to device data and functions than it needs, enabling data harvesting.
Verifying a device's integrity, such as detecting rooting or jailbreaking, before allowing access to sensitive resources.

examTips: Sideloading bypasses app-store vetting; the control is to restrict installation to official stores and check app reputation.
Jailbreaking and rooting disable built-in protections and break the app sandbox; block such devices from sensitive apps via attestation.
MDM or UEM is the exam's default control for enforcing mobile policy, compliance and remote wipe.
BYOD mixes personal and corporate data; containerisation separates them, and COPE or CYOD are alternative models.
Open or rogue Wi-Fi enables interception; require a VPN on untrusted networks and prefer app or hardware authenticators over SMS codes.
videos.realWorld: With mobile as the dominant banking channel in Nigeria, mobile-device vulnerabilities are central to both customer and staff security. Banking apps increasingly perform device attestation and refuse to run on rooted or jailbroken phones, and fraud teams watch for logins from tampered or newly registered devices, a pattern tied to SIM-swap and fake-app fraud. For staff, the SOC relies on MDM or UEM to enforce encryption, patch levels and remote wipe and to block non-compliant devices from corporate resources. GRC sets the mobile and BYOD policy, chooses the deployment model, and defines acceptable use.

quiz.q: A customer installs a banking app from a link sent on WhatsApp rather than the official app store; the app steals their login and OTP. Which mobile vulnerability was primarily exploited?
quiz.explain: Installing an app from outside the official store bypasses store vetting, which is sideloading, and is a common route for fake banking apps. The scenario does not describe removing device restrictions or a Bluetooth attack.

quiz.q: A bank wants to enforce encryption, screen locks and patch levels on staff phones and be able to wipe a lost device remotely. Which technology BEST provides this?
options: Mobile device management (MDM) or unified endpoint management
quiz.explain: MDM or UEM enforces device policy and compliance and supports remote wipe, which is exactly what is required. A WAF protects web apps, a stack canary is a memory-overflow defence, and a storage bucket is unrelated.

quiz.q: Why is a rooted or jailbroken device a greater risk when running a banking app?
options: Removing built-in restrictions breaks the app sandbox and disables protections, exposing the app to malware
quiz.explain: Rooting or jailbreaking disables the platform's security controls and app isolation, letting malware access data the sandbox would normally protect. Screen size, battery use and Wi-Fi are not the security concern, which is why banking apps often block such devices via attestation.

videos.title: Zero-day Vulnerabilities
videos.summary: Messer explains what makes a vulnerability a zero-day, why there is no patch or signature at first, and how defenders reduce risk from something no one yet knows about.
videos.deepDive:
A zero-day vulnerability is a flaw that is unknown to the party responsible for fixing it, typically the software vendor, and therefore has no patch available. The name comes from the idea that defenders have had zero days to prepare. A zero-day exploit is attack code that takes advantage of such a flaw, and a zero-day attack is its use in the wild before a fix exists. The defining property is the knowledge gap: the attacker knows about a weakness that the defender and vendor do not, so every signature-based and patch-based defence is blind to it by definition.

Why are zero-days so prized and so dangerous? Because there is no patch, no vendor advisory and usually no detection signature at the moment of use, a zero-day can bypass defences that are otherwise strong. High-end actors, especially nation-states and well-funded criminal groups, discover or purchase them and use them sparingly against high-value targets to preserve their value, since a zero-day is spent once it is discovered and patched. There is an active market: vendors run bug-bounty programmes to buy flaws and fix them, while brokers and criminal markets buy them to exploit. The window of maximum danger runs from first exploitation until a patch is released and deployed; even after a patch exists, unpatched systems remain exposed, at which point it is no longer strictly a zero-day but is still dangerous.

A worked timeline makes it concrete. An attacker discovers a flaw in a widely used product and quietly builds an exploit. They use it against selected targets; defenders see strange effects but no known signature matches. Eventually a security researcher or victim notices the anomaly, analyses it, and reports it. The vendor develops and releases a patch, and detection signatures follow. Organisations race to patch before opportunistic attackers, now aware of the flaw, exploit the many systems still unpatched. Log4j and several browser and mobile OS flaws have followed exactly this arc.

How a SOC analyst copes with something that has no signature: you cannot detect a zero-day by its known indicators because there are none, so you rely on behaviour and anomalies. EDR and network monitoring look for what the exploit does rather than what it is: a trusted process spawning a shell, unusual outbound connections, unexpected privilege changes, or a service behaving abnormally. Threat intelligence provides early warning once a zero-day is reported. When a vendor issues an emergency patch for an actively exploited flaw, the SOC and vulnerability-management team treat it as a fire drill.

Mitigation accepts that you cannot patch what you do not know about, so it emphasises resilience and defence in depth. Behaviour-based detection (EDR, anomaly detection) can catch exploitation without a signature. Reducing the attack surface, applying least privilege, and segmenting the network limit what any single exploit can reach. Exploit mitigations built into modern operating systems make many flaws harder to exploit even before they are known. A fast, rehearsed patch process shortens the exposure window once a fix appears, and virtual patching via IPS or WAF rules can buy time. For GRC, the message is that zero-day risk is why defence in depth and incident-response readiness exist; no single preventive control is sufficient, and residual risk must be managed and monitored.

keyTerms.def: A flaw unknown to the vendor or defenders, for which no patch yet exists.
Attack code that takes advantage of a zero-day vulnerability before a fix is available.
Use of a zero-day exploit in the wild before the vulnerability is known and patched.
Detecting threats by what they do rather than by known signatures, essential against unknown flaws.
Layering independent controls so that no single unknown flaw leads to full compromise.
Using IPS or WAF rules to block exploitation of a flaw as a temporary measure before a real patch is applied.
Minimising exposed services, features and privileges so an unknown exploit has fewer targets and less reach.

examTips: A zero-day has no patch and no signature because the vendor does not yet know about it; that knowledge gap is the defining trait.
You cannot use signatures against a zero-day, so the detection answer is behaviour-based and anomaly detection, not antivirus signatures.
Zero-days are favoured by well-funded actors such as nation-states, who use them sparingly against high-value targets.
Defence in depth, least privilege, segmentation and OS exploit mitigations reduce zero-day impact even without a patch.
Once a fix is released, unpatched systems are still at risk; fast patching closes the exposure window.
videos.realWorld: When a vendor announces a zero-day under active exploitation, a bank SOC treats it as an emergency: identify exposed assets, apply virtual patching at the IPS or WAF while the real patch is tested, and hunt for the behavioural indicators associated with exploitation. Because there is no signature at first, EDR anomaly detection and threat-intelligence feeds are the front line, and network segmentation limits how far a successful exploit can spread. GRC uses zero-day risk to justify investment in defence in depth and a rehearsed incident-response capability, and reports residual risk and mean-time-to-patch for emergency fixes to the risk committee and CBN examiners.

quiz.q: Attackers exploit a flaw in a widely used product for which the vendor has issued no patch and no security tool has a matching signature. Which term describes this flaw?
quiz.explain: A flaw unknown to the vendor with no patch and no signature is a zero-day vulnerability, which is why existing defences are initially blind to it. The other options are known, addressable weakness types.

quiz.q: Since a zero-day has no known signature, which detection approach is MOST useful for catching its exploitation?
options: Behaviour and anomaly-based detection such as EDR
quiz.explain: Behaviour-based detection identifies malicious activity by what it does, so it can catch exploitation even without a signature. Signature antivirus is blind to unknown flaws, version checks and passwords do not detect exploitation.

quiz.q: Which set of controls BEST reduces the impact of a zero-day even though no patch exists yet?
options: Defence in depth, least privilege and network segmentation
quiz.explain: Layered controls, least privilege and segmentation limit how far any single unknown exploit can reach, providing resilience without a patch. The other options weaken security and increase exposure.

objectives.title: Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity

videos.title: An Overview of Malware
videos.summary: Messer introduces malware as a category, explains how it gets onto a system, and walks through the main families the exam expects you to recognise: ransomware, trojans, worms, spyware, bloatware, viruses, keyloggers, logic bombs and rootkits.
videos.deepDive:
Malware is simply software that does something the owner of the machine did not consent to. The exam cares less about the definition and more about whether you can look at a scenario and name the family. The trick is to classify by how it spreads and what it does once it is running, because those two axes separate almost every type.

Spread mechanisms fall into three groups. A virus attaches itself to a file or program and needs a human to run that file. A worm spreads on its own across a network by exploiting a vulnerability, with no user action at all. A trojan does not spread by itself; it tricks a person into installing it by pretending to be something useful, such as a cracked copy of Microsoft Office or a fake bank statement PDF. Once you fix the spread mechanism in your head, the payload is a separate question. The same trojan might drop a keylogger, a ransomware encryptor or a remote-access tool.

Payload behaviours are what the rest of this objective drills into. Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment. Spyware and keyloggers quietly collect information. A logic bomb waits for a trigger such as a date or an employee record being deleted from HR. A rootkit hides itself and other malware by modifying the operating system or kernel. Bloatware is not strictly malicious but is unwanted software that ships pre-installed and expands the attack surface.

Worked example: a finance officer at a Lagos microfinance bank receives an email that appears to come from a vendor, with an attachment named Invoice_Sept.pdf.exe. She double-clicks it. Nothing visible happens, but the file drops a second executable into C:\Users\Public, adds a Run key in the registry for persistence and begins beaconing to an external IP on port 443 every 60 seconds. Classification: the delivery was a trojan (it pretended to be an invoice). The beaconing behaviour suggests a remote-access payload. If it then starts scanning the LAN on port 445 and copying itself to other hosts, a worm component has been added.

What this looks like to a SOC analyst: the EDR alert fires on a process launched from a user-writable directory, the parent process is Outlook or a browser, and there is a new autorun entry. In the SIEM you would pivot on the host, the user and the destination IP, check whether any other host contacted the same IP, and look at proxy logs for the initial download. Triage moves from confirm it is real (hash lookup, sandbox detonation) to scope it (who else) to contain it (isolate the host through EDR, block the IP and domain at the firewall and proxy).

Mitigation is layered because no single control catches every family: user awareness reduces trojan success, patching kills worms, application allow lists stop unknown executables from launching, EDR watches behaviour rather than signatures, and tested offline backups make ransomware survivable. On the exam, when a scenario says the malware arrived disguised as legitimate software, answer trojan; when it moved across the network with no clicks, answer worm; when it needed a file to be opened, answer virus.

keyTerms.def: Any software intentionally designed to damage, disrupt, spy on or gain unauthorised access to a system.
Malware disguised as legitimate software that relies on the user to install it and does not self-replicate.
Self-replicating malware that spreads across networks by exploiting vulnerabilities without any user action.
Malware that attaches to a file or program and replicates only when a user executes the infected host file.
The part of malware that performs the actual malicious action once the malware is running.
A technique such as a registry Run key or scheduled task that lets malware survive a reboot.
The channel malware uses to receive instructions from and send data to an attacker-controlled server.
A small initial program whose only job is to install other malware on the system.

examTips: Classify by spread first: needs a user to run a file = virus, spreads alone over the network = worm, pretends to be useful software = trojan.
A scenario describing regular outbound connections at fixed intervals to an unknown external IP is pointing at command-and-control beaconing.
Do not confuse bloatware with malware; bloatware is unwanted and risky but not designed to be malicious.
The exam frequently combines families, for example a trojan that installs a rootkit; answer based on the specific behaviour the question asks about.
videos.realWorld: In a bank SOC, most malware cases start as an EDR or email-gateway alert rather than a user report. The analyst confirms the file hash against threat intelligence, checks whether the process tree makes sense (a spreadsheet spawning PowerShell does not), then scopes across the estate before isolating the host. GRC teams care about the same case from a different angle: was the control that failed documented, is there a CBN or NDPA notification duty if customer data was touched, and does the incident register capture the root cause for the next audit?

quiz.q: A user downloads what appears to be a free PDF converter from a forum. After installation the SOC observes the host making outbound HTTPS connections to an unknown IP every 30 seconds. No other hosts are affected. Which type of malware best describes the initial infection?
quiz.explain: The user was tricked into installing software that looked useful, which is the definition of a trojan. A worm would spread to other hosts on its own, a virus needs an infected host file, and a logic bomb waits for a trigger condition rather than beaconing immediately.

quiz.q: Overnight, 40 servers in a data centre become infected with no user interaction. Investigation shows the malware exploited an unpatched SMB vulnerability to copy itself between hosts. What is this?
quiz.explain: Self-replication across the network with no user action by exploiting a vulnerability is the defining behaviour of a worm. Trojans require a user to install them, rootkits hide malware rather than spread it, and spyware collects data.

quiz.q: An analyst finds a new registry Run key pointing to an executable in a user's temp folder. What is the primary purpose of this artefact from the attacker's perspective?
quiz.explain: A Run key causes the executable to launch each time the user logs in, which keeps the malware alive after a reboot. That is persistence. It does not by itself raise privileges, move data out or reach other hosts.

videos.title: Viruses and Worms
videos.summary: Messer contrasts viruses, which need a user to run an infected file, with worms, which self-propagate across networks, and describes sub-types such as boot sector, script, macro and fileless viruses.
videos.deepDive:
The single most tested distinction in this section is that a virus requires human action and a worm does not. Everything else is detail layered on top of that.

A virus is code that inserts itself into another file or program. When the user opens that file, the virus runs, then usually copies itself into other files so it survives and spreads. Sub-types are named after where they live. A program virus infects executables. A boot sector virus writes itself into the master boot record so it loads before the operating system. A script virus is written in JavaScript, VBScript or PowerShell and runs inside a browser or the Windows Script Host. A macro virus lives inside an Office document and runs when macros are enabled; this is why Microsoft now blocks macros from internet-sourced files by default. A fileless virus never writes a file to disk at all; it runs in memory, typically through PowerShell or WMI, and persists through the registry or scheduled tasks. Fileless malware matters because traditional antivirus scans files on disk and has nothing to scan.

A worm carries its own propagation engine. It scans for reachable hosts, checks whether each one is vulnerable to a specific exploit, delivers the exploit, and repeats from the new host. Because there is no human in the loop, worms move at machine speed. WannaCry in 2017 used the EternalBlue SMB exploit to compromise around 200,000 systems in a day; many of those systems had a patch available for two months. The worm carried a ransomware payload, which is why you will see it described as both.

Worked example of a macro virus in a bank: a credit analyst receives Loan_Book_Q3.xlsm from what looks like a colleague. She enables content. The macro uses Shell to run an encoded PowerShell command that downloads a second-stage payload. In the SIEM this appears as EXCEL.EXE spawning powershell.exe with a -EncodedCommand argument (Sysmon Event ID 1 or Windows Security 4688 with command-line auditing on). That parent-child relationship is the signature; Excel has no legitimate reason to launch PowerShell.

Worm indicators are different. You would see one host suddenly generating thousands of connection attempts to port 445 or 3389 across the subnet (firewall or NetFlow logs), IDS signatures for the exploit firing repeatedly, and then the same behaviour appearing on the hosts it reached. The spread pattern itself is the indicator, and speed of containment matters more than perfect analysis. A SOC analyst would block the port at the internal segmentation firewall, isolate the source host, and then work backwards.

Mitigation for viruses is mostly about the human and the endpoint: security awareness, blocking macros and script hosts by policy, and EDR that watches process behaviour rather than just file hashes. Mitigation for worms is mostly about the network: patch the exploited vulnerability, segment the network so one subnet cannot reach every other, and disable unneeded services so there is nothing to exploit. On the exam, if the scenario mentions patching as the fix, it is nearly always a worm.

keyTerms.def: A virus that infects the master boot record so it executes before the operating system loads.
A virus written in the macro language of an application such as Microsoft Office and triggered when the document's macros run.
A virus written in a scripting language such as PowerShell, VBScript or JavaScript.
Malware that runs entirely in memory using built-in tools like PowerShell, leaving no executable on disk for antivirus to scan.
The ability of a worm to locate and infect new hosts without any human involvement.
The SMBv1 exploit used by the WannaCry worm in 2017 to spread across unpatched Windows systems.
Using tools already present on the system, such as PowerShell or WMI, to avoid dropping detectable files.

examTips: User double-clicked, opened, enabled content or ran something = virus. Spread with zero user action = worm.
Fileless malware is tested as the reason signature-based antivirus fails; the answer is behaviour-based EDR.
Macro virus scenarios usually mention Office documents and enabling content or macros.
If the remediation in the answer choices is patching or network segmentation, the question is describing a worm.
videos.realWorld: SOC analysts in fintechs spend a lot of time on Office-spawns-PowerShell alerts, because macro-based delivery is still one of the cheapest ways for criminals to get a foothold. A good detection rule looks at the parent process, the command-line flags and whether the script contacts the internet. Worm-style spread is rarer but far more dangerous, so segmentation between the card-processing network and the office LAN is something GRC teams verify during PCI DSS assessments and CBN risk-based supervision reviews.

quiz.q: A SIEM alert shows winword.exe launching powershell.exe with an encoded command shortly after a user opened an email attachment. There is no new file on disk. Which two descriptions fit this activity?
quiz.explain: A Word document launching PowerShell points to a macro virus, and the absence of any file on disk with execution in memory is the definition of fileless malware. Nothing in the scenario indicates self-propagation, a hidden kernel component or a trigger condition.

quiz.q: Within one hour, hundreds of workstations across multiple offices are compromised. Logs show each infected host scanning the subnet on TCP 445 before the next hosts become infected. Which action would have most directly prevented this?
options: Applying the vendor patch for the exploited SMB vulnerability
quiz.explain: The behaviour is a worm exploiting an SMB vulnerability. Patching removes the vulnerability the worm relies on. Disk encryption and password managers do not stop remote exploitation, and macros are irrelevant because no user action was involved.

quiz.q: Why does traditional signature-based antivirus often miss fileless malware?
options: Fileless malware runs only on Linux
There is no executable written to disk for the scanner to inspect
Fileless malware disables the antivirus service first
quiz.explain: Signature-based antivirus scans files on disk. Fileless malware executes in memory through legitimate tools such as PowerShell, so there is nothing on disk to match a signature against. The other options are not general properties of fileless malware.

videos.title: Spyware and Bloatware
videos.summary: Messer explains spyware as software that secretly monitors the user and sends data to a third party, and bloatware as unwanted pre-installed software that wastes resources and widens the attack surface.
videos.deepDive:
Spyware and bloatware sit at opposite ends of a spectrum. Spyware is designed to harm you by watching you. Bloatware is not designed to harm you, but it makes your system easier to harm. The exam tests whether you can tell them apart and whether you know why bloatware still matters.

Spyware collects information without consent and sends it somewhere. Common forms include browser monitoring that records every site visited, keyloggers that capture keystrokes (covered in the next video), and identity-theft tools that scrape saved passwords, browser cookies and autofill data. Spyware usually arrives bundled with something the user wanted: a free screen recorder, a cracked game, a browser toolbar that promises coupons. Some spyware is commercial, marketed as parental monitoring or employee monitoring, and becomes malicious only because it is installed without the target's knowledge; this category is sometimes called stalkerware.

How spyware behaves once running: it hooks into the browser or the operating system to observe activity, stores what it captures in a local file or in memory, and periodically uploads to a collection server. That upload is your best detection opportunity. Spyware on a bank teller's workstation might upload a few hundred kilobytes every hour to a domain registered three days ago. In proxy logs you would see repeated POST requests to an unfamiliar host, often at very regular intervals, from a process that is not a browser. Windows Event 4688 with command-line logging, or Sysmon Event 3 (network connection), lets you tie the connection to the process.

Bloatware is the trial antivirus, the vendor update utility, the games and the promotional apps that ship on a new laptop or phone. Three problems follow. First, it consumes CPU, memory and disk, which slows the machine and sometimes causes users to disable security tools they blame for the slowness. Second, every extra program is extra code that may contain vulnerabilities; the 2015 Superfish incident is the textbook case, where a pre-installed advertising tool on Lenovo laptops shipped with a self-signed root certificate and its private key, allowing anyone to intercept HTTPS traffic on those machines. Third, bloatware often runs with high privileges and auto-updates from vendor servers, which is exactly the kind of trusted channel supply-chain attackers like to hijack.

Worked SOC scenario: a compliance officer reports her laptop is slow. The analyst checks the process list and finds 14 startup items, including a vendor photo app, a trial VPN, and a browser extension called Deal Finder. The extension is uploading the URL of every page she visits, including internal SharePoint links, to an ad-tech domain. The photo app is a year out of date and has a known privilege-escalation flaw. Classification: the extension is spyware, the rest is bloatware. Remediation is removal, followed by a policy decision.

Mitigation for both is the same discipline. Build a standard image that contains only approved software and re-image new hardware rather than using the vendor build.
